Registered Office: Charles House, 108-110 Finchley Road, London NW3 5JJ January 2012 Vol 39 No 7 ### Royalties _p 2_ Mining royalties and taxation have received a lot of press coverage in recent months as resource rich countries look to secure a larger share of the revenues from their mineral production, including copper and its main by-products gold and silver. In this article we give an overview of royalty rates in key copper mining countries and highlight the main changes that have either come into force or are proposed. ### Aluminium’s woes may be copper’s gain _p 10_ With at least 30% of world aluminium smelting capacity losing money at today’s LME prices of US$2,200/t, the world’s major aluminium producers have been compelled to announce significant permanent closures or temporary idling of their high cost plants. Alcoa, Rio Tinto and Norsk Hydro have so far announced closures while Rio Tinto has also been hit by technical failures and a labour dispute. ZALCO is the Netherlands has gone bankrupt while ALRO in Romania has cut output because of electricity shortages. All these constrain aluminium rod supply (particularly at smelters with captive hot metal casting lines) at a time when substitution pressures had favoured growing usage over copper in insulated wire and cable applications due to a current price ratio of 3.8:1. 2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com

-- End of picture text --> 2 www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES January **2012** ### Royalties ##### Introduction Mining companies now place resource nationalisation high on their list of risks when considering mine project development. Many governments are now looking to secure the benefits of their countries’ natural resources, rather than seeing them exported in the profits of multinational companies. In order to do this they are seeking to take a larger share of the revenues from their mineral production, including copper and its main by-products gold and silver, through higher levels of taxation. Many countries are reviewing royalties and taxation and a number have either increased royalty rates or have announced plans to do so. This has mostly been less developed or developing nations which are trying to raise revenues to finance their development. Countries that have hit the headlines have included Peru, Chile, Zambia, Australia and Poland, but increases have also been announced in Ecuador, Mongolia and Kazakhstan, in order to reap the benefits from new projects under development, while the governments of Indonesia and the Philippines are also looking to increase rates. In this article we give a brief overview of royalty rates for copper worldwide and discuss the recent developments and changes in mineral royalty rates. Tables show the royalty rates for copper and associated products in the key copper producing countries. ##### Royalty rates range from 2% up to 35% The chart below compares royalty rates for copper across countries. Rates are lowest in Brazil, Panama, the DRC, Philippines (subject to change) Papua New Guinea and Spain and highest in Mongolia. In some countries, including Finland and Sweden there is no royalty payable. In Mongolia a two-tier system was introduced in 2011, with a basic rate of 5% and a surtax that varies with the price but can be as high as 30%. The highest flat rate is in the Northern Territories of Australia, although currently there are no copper mines in operation in the state. In a number of countries the rates are within a band, with the exact level determined by various factors, the most common of which is the metal price. Within Australia rates vary from state to state, but are below 5% in all states with the exception of the Northern Territories where they are 20%. Rates also vary by province in Canada and by jurisdiction in Argentina, while in Laos and Ecuador they are agreed on a case by case basis. Royalty rates by country

2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES January 2012 3 In most countries, royalties are on an ad valorem basis rather than being a fixed value, but the basis for assessment varies. Typically they are either based on mine gat

e value, sales revenue, or, in a few cases, profits. In India they are based on the value of the contained metal. If based on mine gate value, then the smelting and refining costs are allowable, while if payable on sales revenue then cost of transport and direct marketing costs may also be allowable. If based on profits, then all production costs are allowable. In some countries the royalty rate is on a sliding scale, with the rate dependent on factors such as the copper price, the size of the operation, the value of the product or the size of profits. The latter two will to some extent depend on the prices for copper and its by-products. This enables the country to benefit from high metals prices, while ensuring that the producers are not squeezed in times of low prices. ##### Peru – new leftist government seeks funds for social projects In Peru, the newly elected government approved a new system for royalty payments in September 2011. The election of the left-leaning Ollanta Humala to the Peruvian presidency in June had caused some concern among mining companies either already operating or developing projects in Peru, due to his past record of support for the nationalisation of mines and statements that he had made during the election campaign expressing his intent to impose higher taxes on miners. The finance minister Luis Castilla stated that the new system would raise additional revenue to fund anti-poverty initiatives and social programmes to help the poorest sector of the population, fulfilling an election promise. Under the new legislation, mining companies will pay royalties on operating profits in addition to a special mining income tax. Companies subject to Peruvian taxation benefit from stable tax rates as they sign a tax stability agreement which sets out the tax rate that will be paid regardless of changes that are made to tax rates. Companies with a stability agreement will continue to pay the 30% special mining income tax as specified in the agreements plus royalty rates on profits that may range from 4% to 13%. Companies without a stability agreement will pay between 1% and 12% of operating profits in addition to a new mining income tax. Previously royalties were paid at between 1% and 3% of net sales. One amendment introduces a temporary increase in the royalty rates in order to raise funds to finance reconstruction following the massive earthquake in February 2010. The ruling party does not have a majority in the Congress and the initiative faced strong opposition when it was originally introduced earlier in the year. The old royalty scheme consisted of a fixed rate of 5% (or 4% if a royalty fix agreement was made before December 2004) of operating income and a variable rate depending on profitability. The amendment only applies to operations producing more than 50,000t of copper. Miners will pay 5% when their margins are less than or equal to 35% and the rate will increase on a sliding scale up to 14% when operating margins are 85% or higher. The new royalty comes into effect immediately for new operations and from 2018 for all mines. Mines already operating were offered the possibility of voluntarily entering into a transitional rate of 4-9% for 2011 and 2012, returning to the old scheme for 2013-2017 and then getting a new six-year stability contract for the 2018-2023 period. This would enable funds to be raised immediately to support the reconstruction. The option was open until January 17th of this year, and in early January major miners Escondida and Antofagasta both announced that they had accepted the new system. Financially, those most at risk from the new system are expected to be projects due on stream in the latter part of this decade, particularly the more marginal projects. ##### Brazil to change the base for evaluating royalty payments Brazil’s new mining code is to be sent to Congress for ratification in early 2012. The new code contains three bills for the regulation of the mining sector. One bill will involve a change to royalty payments, known locally as the CREM tax, while the other two will establish new rules for prospecting and mining concessions and create a new agency to regulate the sector. Under the new system, royalty revenues are expected to more than double from an estimated 1.3B reais in 2011 to 3B reais. The main change is that royalties will be charged on gross sales revenue rather than on net sales as is currently the case. This change will result in payments nearly doubling. In addition royalty rates are set to increase, although the exact levels have not

yet been announced for all commodities.  Rates will range from 0.5% to 6%, with the rate for iron ore rising from 2% to 4%.  The rate for copper is currently 2%. 

In addition, in December 2011 the assembly of the state of Parб approved a new tax on all minerals produced locally, under which mineral extraction will be taxed at a rate of 6.45 reais per tonne.  Vale’s currently producing copper mine, Sossego, as well as its projects Salobo and Cristalino are all located in Parб state.  The company’s most productive iron ore complex, Carajбs, is also located in the state and the company is considering taking legal action, declaring that the creation and collection of new mining taxes by the states is unconstitutional. Meanwhile, the assembly of Minas Gerais state has approved the introduction of a new tax on mineral exports.  The tax will be applied to foreign exports and shipments to other Brazilian states.  It is proposed that mineral exports are taxed 2.1813 reais (US$1.23) per tonne, with the exception of gold and ionium. Small miners and minerals destined for industrialisation in the state will also be exempt, except if they are intended for packaging, processing, pelletizing, sintering or similar processes.  The objective of the new tax is to fund environmental cleanup programmes and mine supervision. The state government also hopes the measure will encourage companies to invest in adding value to the ore mined in the state.

##### Ecuador agrees parameters, debate continues in Panama 

At the end of November a range was established for royalty rates for new mining projects in Ecuador. Non-renewable natural resources minister Wilson Pastor announced that rates would be between 5% and 8%.  Individual negotiations will take place with companies to set company specific rates, which will also depend on metals prices.  The two major projects under development are Kinross Gold’s Fruta del Norte gold project and Ecuacorriente’s Mirador copper-gold project.  It had been expected that contracts would be signed by the end of December or early in January 2012.  The mining authorities’ goals in setting the contracts are: to promote exploration and mining, guarantee state participation, define reasonable profits for the investments, reinvest royalties in social projects in mining areas and establish clear and secure investment regulations.  The government is also demanding advance payments on royalties, the revenue from which will be used for social projects, including schools and roads. 

The situation in Panama, where Inmet is investing in the Petaquilla project remains unclear, although it was announced in May 2011 that the company had agreed royalty rates of 2% for both gold and copper. In July 2010, planned modifications to the mining code were announced, including an increase in royalty rates from 2% to 4%.  Taxes will be payable as so

on as a company starts to generate revenue from an operation. However the new law was repealed in March 2011, bringing royalty rates back to 2%. ##### Zambia to double copper royalty Following the presidential elections in September 2011, concern was expressed by mining companies operating in the country over the possible new legislation and taxation. However the government has since declared that it has no plans to renationalise the mining industry, and has also reneged on its preelection promises to introduce a windfall tax on mining company profits. The chamber of mines and other key players in the industry have expressed concern over the possible negative impact on the mining industry of such measures. However it was announced in November 2011 that the mineral royalty on base metals will be doubled to 6% and that on precious metals will be raised from 5% to 6%. The finance minister has said that the increase, together with a change in the tax on mining income, will raise about $195M for the country, which will be used to increase social spending and farming subsidies. Currently, although copper accounts for 70 percent of Zambia's foreign exchange earnings, it only contributes about 10 percent to the gross domestic product and less than 3 percent to the country's tax regime. It is interesting to note that the royalty has increased from just 0.6% in 2008. More recently, responding to pressure from international mining companies, the government has said that the rates will be reviewed if metal prices decline significantly in the future. The Zambian government has also agreed to reduce an export duty on copper and cobalt concentrates from 15 percent to 10 percent as a way of encouraging local value addition and creating jobs. ###### Mining royalties - Africa ||**Element**|**Rate**|**Type and basis**|**Allowances**| |---|---|---|---|---| |Botsw ana|base metals|3%|ad alorem on gross market value at

It will also defer the removal of the zero-rating for value added tax on mineral exports, and cut a proposed export tax from 5% to between 0% and 2% depending on the industry. Namibia’s main mineral expo

##### Kazakhstan introduces new mineral production tax 

In 2009 Kazakhstan introduced a new mineral production tax to replace its royalty system.  The rates are on a sliding scale and depend on the level of production, rising as production increases.  However the rates are significantly higher than the former royalty rates, ranging from 7% up to 20%, compared with 2- 6%.  There was a phase-in period over the 3 years 2009-2011.  The tax applies to the value of the product produced. 

##### Mongolia 

With the development of the Oyu Tolgoi copper and gold mine proceeding and start up now expected in 2013, the government of Mongolia is keen to increase the financial returns from its metals mining industry.  A new two tier royalty scheme was passed by the government in November 2010 and introduced from January 2011.  The base rate is 5% for both copper and gold, as for other metals, but a steep additional surtax royalty has been imposed to replace the former windfall tax.  This surtax is on a sliding scale and depends on metal prices.  For copper and molybdenum, the rate also depends on the level of processing that the material has undergone before it is sold, i.e. it is charged on either copper in ore, copper in concentrate or refined copper metal.

The royalty is charged on the total sales value.  For Oyu Tolgoi, and existing producer Erdenet, both concentrate producers, the tax will be/is charged on the total sales value of the concentrate, and at the current price level is 13%, resulting in a total tax rate of 18%. 

##### Indonesia and Philippines both seek to increase revenue from royalties 

The Energy and Mines minister of Indonesia has said that the country will seek to increase the royalties paid by mining companies by renegotiating contracts.  Currently royalty rates for copper are stated as 4%, for gold 3.75% and for silver 3.25%.  However these have been negotiated in the contract of work (COW), which allows the company to carry out its operations, and may vary from these rates quoted.  In many cases they are lower.  The government is proposing to renegotiate these contracts and increase the royalty rates at the same time.  The royalty is an ad valorem rate payable on production.  In addition there is a 10% tax payable on profits.

proposed that a 5% royalty payable against profits is introduced to replace the current 2% excise duty on net profits. It also plans to increase the number of operations that are liable to pay the royalty, and the finance department is investigating a proposal to declare all mining sites as mineral reservations (MRs) that would then be liable to pay the tax. Under existing Philippine legislation, products derived from mineral reservations are considered to be of strategic value and so the producers are compelled to pay tax. Currently there are nine existing MRs, none of which are copper mining areas. However the MGB targeted an additional 15 sites to be proclaimed as MRs in 2011, including areas producing copper, gold and nickel. ##### Australia back tracked on resource tax for non ferrous metals producers In May 2010 the Australian government announced proposals for a 40% mineral resources tax on the profits of the producers of non-renewable mineral resources. The news was greeted with dismay and concern by the mining industry, and a number of major producers, including Xstrata and BHP announced that they would be reviewing their project pipeline. Indeed, Xstrata put on hold the proposed underground development of its Ernest Henry mine, a project that would extend the life of the mine. There was considerable concern that the tax would stifle investment in the industry and the development of new resources. After weeks of debate the government bowed to criticism and announced amendments to the original proposal. The tax will now be applied at 30%, and will only apply to profits from coal and iron ore operations. Non ferrous metals producers were able to breathe again, and Xstrata reversed its decision over the development at Ernest Henry, which is now coming into production. ##### Polish producer KGHM to be hit by new mining tax In November 2011 the Polish government announced plans for a new mining tax that will hit copper and silver producer KGHM hard. The aim is to raise revenue for the country’s economic development and to reduce the government deficit. More details of the tax were announced in December, and, following an appeal by KGHM to the government to reduce its potential liability, the proposed rates were amended. The tax will be payable per tonne of copper and kg of silver extracted and the rate will vary with metals prices. CRU estimates that consumption of aluminium in these applications totalled 4.7 million tonnes in 2011, an impressive 16% year-on-year rise due to booming global demand for bare aluminium overhead conductors and substitution gains in insulated wires and cables due to the high price and volatility of copper. But while world aluminium demand has held up well in 2011, the other key aluminium industry metrics have been moving adversely. From a quarterly average peak of US$2,600/t in Q2 2011, LME cash prices fell to US$2,399/t in Q3 and then down to US$2,090/t in Q4 and at present, LME prices are hovering around US$2,200/t. The problem is that at these levels as almost 30% of the world aluminium smelting industry is loss making based on a C1 cash cost basis according to CRU estimates. The cost structure breakdown of the aluminium industry is broadly 33% alumina (the primary raw material), 33% energy (mainly electricity), and 33% other costs (other raw materials, labour and other costs). The main driver of the current crisis is that aluminium prices have been falling at a time when electricity prices (except those from hydroelectric or geothermal sources) have been rising due to the general upward trend in energy inputs (oil, gas, coal). There has also been the cost burden of investment in renewable energy sources (wind, solar, tidal) which is more expensive than traditional energy sources and the legacy de-commissioning costs of nuclear reactors. The need to prepare to meet more stringent guidelines on CO2 emissions is also an additional cost pressure. Another obvious indicator of the cr

isis is the severe overproduction relative to demand. LME inventories of primary aluminium are just over 5 million metric tonnes, while total industry stocks, including IAI producer stocks, SHFE inventories, government stockpiles and estimates of unreported stocks bring the total stock overhang to almost 12 million tonnes. These levels are astronomical in the context of world annual primary aluminium demand of 45 million tonnes in 2011. Not surprisingly the last three months have seen the pressure on aluminium industry profitability begin to bite very hard. In mid-October the Romanian vertically integrated primary and processed aluminium producer **ALRO** , announced that it shutdown one pot line and had brought forward the decommissioning of cell pots that were approaching their scheduled maintenance time. On the 17th October **Rio Tinto** announced that six Australian and New Zealand assets had been transferred into its Pacific Aluminium subsidiary and that seven other non-core assets have now also been transferred out of its Rio Tinto Alcan subsidiary. These assets are to be managed and run separately from Rio Tinto Alcan while the Group investigates divestment options. The Australian government’s carbon tax implementation plan is likely to be faster than previously expected and this will raise power costs for Australia’s coal fired smelters placing the assets at risk if metal prices remain low. This is behind the decision. On the 16th December Rio Tinto followed this up with an announcement that it intended to close its Lynemouth aluminium smelter in the UK by the end of February 2012. A power failure in December had already cut its capacity of 181,000tpy by two-thirds. In Canada, a circuit breaker failure at Rio Tinto’s Shawinigan aluminium at the end of December reduced capacity at the plant by 50% to 50,000tpy. The company had already decided to permanently end operations at the site by December 2014, but has yet to decide if it will restart the smelting cells before production at the facility is wound down. Meanwhile on January 1st 2012 Rio Tinto initiated a lock out at its Canadian Alma smelter and integrated

aluminium wire rod plant after a labour contract expired on 31<sup>st</sup> December.  This shut down two-thirds, or 292,000tpy, of the smelter’s capacity after prolonged labour negotiations failed to reach an agreement.  Rio Tinto declared _force majeure_ due to the combination of the two issues and customers were told that they might see delayed orders or extended delivery dates. One local rod consumer said, “ _It has certainly upset the market.  Alma’s rod wheel is idle and so it does have an impact.  The reaction was immediate.  For the last six to nine months, the market was tight anyway. This only adds severely to that pain. Someone is going to have to bring rod into this country_ ”. 

The combination of all these actions meant that a total of 462,000 tonnes of annual smelter capacity had been idled or closed by Rio Tinto.  There are also disputes over power tariffs for Rio Tinto Alcan’s 267,000tpy Sebree smelter in the USA and at St Jean-de-Maurienne in France and if these cannot be resolved then the future of these operations would also come into question. But in early-December the Group also announced a US$3.3bn project to modernise its low cost Kitimat aluminium smelter in British Columbia, Canada which would increase its smelter capacity by 48% to 420,000tpy by 2014. 

On 13<sup>th</sup> December Dutch primary aluminium producer **ZALCO** went bankrupt. It had a capacity of 224,000tpy at its smelter in Vlissingen which employed 500 people. One of the two official receivers said in an interview that, “The company went bankrupt on Tuesday and on Friday we decided to shut down the plant due to lack of funds; we couldn’t pay the energy bills”. 

On January 9<sup>th</sup> 2012 **Alcoa** announced its results for 2011.  In Q4 it reported a loss from continuing operations of US$193m.  Alcoa predicts a 7% rise in global aluminium demand in 2012 compared to growth of 13% in 2010 and 10% in 2011.  Growing demand for aluminium combined with production related cutbacks will result in a global market deficit of 600,000t in 2012 it estimates.  Alcoa has said it is idling 531,000tpy or 12% of its smelting capacity and permanently closing its 219,000tpy Tennessee smelter due to declining prices. The smelter was idled in 2009 along with two of six idled pot lines at its Rockdale smelter in Texas.  Alcoa is also curtailing output at three European smelters.  Operations at its 150,000tpy Portovesme plant in Italy will be shut permanently while those of its 87,000tpy La Coruna smelter (with rod mill) and 93,000tpy Aviles smelter in Spain will be temporarily idled during H1 2012. 

Two days later Norwegian headquartered **Norsk Hydro** said it was curtailing one third of its 180,000tpy capacity at its Australian smelter in Kurri Kurri with the loss of 150 out of 500 jobs.  The

Meanwhile in **China** almost 20% of aluminium smelter capacity will lie idle in 2012, due to rising energy costs and falling aluminium prices.  Output will reach an estimated 21.6m tonnes in 2012 but capacity by the end of this year could be as high as 27m tonnes.  There have been limited production cutbacks in Henan and South West China due to power shortages, but these have been more than offset by a rapid growth in greenfield projects in the Northern provinces.  The government has announced that aluminium smelter output will be capped at 24m tonnes by 2015, however these national targets are usually collectively exceed by ambitious regional provinces.  It has stepped up efforts to slow metal production growth to curb surging raw material prices, protect the environment and contain inflation.  It is taking measures to conserve electricity use after missing its energy reduction target in its last 5 year plan. 

However in the **Gulf** , **Dubal** expects its profits to rise by between 30-35% in 2011.  Its net profit in 2010 was US$580m. **Maaden** is also in the process of building a huge integrated alumina refinery, aluminium smelter (capacity 740,000tpy) and flat rolled products plant in **Saudi Arabia** designed to make the Gulf the hub for primary aluminium and semi-manufactures in the Middle East.  Access to cheap and sustainable power is the main key to profitable aluminium smelting. 

Recent price movements starkly highlight the imminent problems faced by smelter operations in the top 50% of the cost curve.  12 million tonnes of primary aluminium inventories will take some years to be consumed.  Smelter cutbacks, especially those which have integrated aluminium rod mills, will inevitably lead to lower aluminium rod supply from these facilities, while aluminium cutbacks will generally have some knock on effect on aluminium wirerod output and annual and spot premiums.  This may frustrate the insulated cable industry and its customer’s desire to substitute cheaper aluminium wire and cable for more expensive copper wire and cable in those applications where they are interchangeable.  Demand for aluminium rod for bare overhead conductor manufacture remains very strong globally so this will likely absorb the vast majority of decreasing aluminium rod supply, leaving little left over for insulated cablemakers to substitute for more expensive copper rod.  So in the short term substitution pressures will likely diminish due to declining rod availability despite a copper: aluminium price ratio of 3.8:1.
